hero.alt: Satya Nadella on the Ignite stage under three panels reading 'Where you build', 'Where your data lives' and 'Where your agents go to work'
hero.caption: Satya Nadella frames Microsoft's AI platform: where you build, where your data lives, and where your agents go to work

items.alt: Copilot app showing an open pipeline chart by stage, at-risk opportunities, and a Workspace panel listing four completed steps using Salesforce, Outlook Mail and Teams plugins
items.title: Copilot runs a sales review across three systems
items.what: Asked to review the forecast, Copilot pulled the West region pipeline from Salesforce, compared it with last week, traced the change and flagged deals at risk. The Workspace panel shows each step and the plugins used (Salesforce, Outlook Mail and Teams). It then recommends reopening the biggest stalled deal and offers to message the account owner in Teams.
items.means: This is what 'Copilot as the operating system for work' looks like in practice. The analysis a sales manager spends Monday morning assembling arrives as one answer, with its sources and steps shown, so you can check it before you act.

items.alt: Autopilot start screen with a standing instruction to track client outreach and draft follow-ups, and a 'What's been happening' timeline of completed tasks
items.title: Autopilot takes standing instructions
items.what: The user sets one instruction: track fundraising outreach, client news and service cases for three clients, draft a follow-up if a client hasn't replied in a week, and bring a weekly performance summary. The timeline shows Autopilot sending a morning brief, preparing client-meeting briefs and logging conversations in Dynamics 365, each reviewed by the user.
items.means: This is delegation rather than assistance: you set the rule once and approve the results. Briefing and supervising an agent becomes part of the job, much as delegating to a junior colleague is today.

items.alt: Copilot reasoning panel showing 'Using Hybrid Intelligence', checking files on the PC, then producing an overview of NRF 2027
items.title: Copilot works with files on your own PC
items.what: Asked for an overview of an upcoming retail conference, Copilot used 'Hybrid Intelligence' to search the web and check files stored locally on the PC, including a speaker-guidance PDF, before writing its answer.
items.means: AI no longer needs everything uploaded to the cloud first. Combining local files with online sources makes Copilot useful for the documents that live on people's laptops, and it raises new questions for IT about what an assistant can read.

items.alt: Microsoft IQ preview listing business plugins such as Retail Quote to Order, Month-End Close, Warranty and Returns and Supply Chain Operations, each with an owner and description
items.title: Company know-how gets packaged as plugins
items.what: Microsoft IQ shows a catalogue of business plugins for a demo company: Quote to Order, Month-End Close, Warranty and Returns, Supply Chain Operations and more. Each has a named owner and a description of the process and systems it covers, and some are marked 'Certified'.
items.means: How your organisation actually works (who approves what, which system is the record) becomes a reusable asset that every agent can draw on. The people who document and own these processes become more valuable, not less.

items.alt: Agent 365 Business Analytics drilling from Research and Discovery down to Statistical analysis plans, showing sessions, cost, AI value, active users and assisted hours for each level
items.title: AI gets an ROI dashboard
items.what: Agent 365 Business Analytics breaks AI use down from department to individual task. In the demo, Research & Discovery shows 7.8K sessions costing $38.8K against $100.1K of estimated AI value and 1.4K assisted hours, and you can drill down to a single use case such as statistical analysis plans.
items.means: AI spending stops being a leap of faith. Leaders can see which tasks pay off and which don't, and anyone running an AI rollout will be expected to present numbers like these.

items.alt: Microsoft 365 admin center page 'Agents without recent activity' showing 2,600 inactive agents, cleanup actions over time and automations to notify owners, block and delete agents
items.title: IT gets a clean-up crew for idle agents
items.what: The admin center lists 2,600 inactive agents created in Foundry, Copilot Studio or Agent Builder, with counts that were blocked, deleted or excluded. Automations notify owners of inactive agents, block them, and delete agents that stay blocked for 30 days.
items.means: Agent sprawl is the new shadow IT. Anyone can now build an agent, so someone has to track, review and retire them, and that lifecycle work becomes routine for IT teams.

items.alt: Alaska Airlines maintenance demo in Foundry comparing a baseline model at 87% accuracy and $92 a month, an optimised prompt at 94% and $370, and a fine-tuned MAI-Code-2-Flash model at 97% and $2
items.title: Fine-tuning: more accurate and far cheaper
items.what: In an Alaska Airlines maintenance demo (run on synthetic data), a classifier went from 87% accuracy at $92 a month, to 94% at $370 with a longer optimised prompt, to 97% at $2 a month after fine-tuning Microsoft's MAI-Code-2-Flash model. That's 227 times cheaper than the optimised version.
items.means: The cheapest way to make AI better at your job isn't always a bigger model. Small models trained on your own data can beat the giants on narrow, repetitive tasks, which makes specialised AI affordable for far more teams.
